issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a civilian in a war zone, broad self-blame for the event is hard to reconcile unless there are other items indicating a specific morally injurious or preventable action. The rest of the profile centers on external danger cues (being followed/watched, loud sounds, checking safety) and vulnerability, not guilt-linked processing. This appraisal is therefore the main clinically questionable item in the set.

vignette:
Layla was 44, a married Middle Eastern woman who worked as a prosecutor, and when she first described what had happened, she did so in a flat, careful way that made it clear how much she had learned to keep herself composed. During a period of civil unrest in her home city, she had been outside a courthouse building when violence broke out nearby and the streets around her office became unstable and frighteningly unpredictable. What stayed with her was not a single dramatic instant so much as the sustained experience of moving through a place that had begun to feel openly unsafe, with people and sounds she could not control. In the months since, certain voices had taken on a sharp significance for her, especially when they sounded like someone connected to that period or carried the same urgent, agitated tone she remembered from the war zone. Hearing a related voice in passing, even at a distance, could make her freeze for a moment and look up quickly, trying to place it before she could let herself relax.

In the immediate aftermath, Layla noticed that ordinary movement through public spaces felt different to her. She had come to notice the sensation of being watched or followed, even in settings where nothing overt was happening, and she would find herself checking who was behind her as she moved from the parking lot into her office or from the office into the elevator. She did not describe this as a belief she could argue with; rather, it was a bodily certainty that arrived before she had time to think. At work, where she still functioned professionally and attended to cases, she became especially tense when leaving late or walking alone between buildings, scanning reflections in glass doors and slowing near corners. Her home had also changed in meaning. She and her husband had once moved easily between rooms and windows, but now there were only a very limited number of places where she felt fully safe, and even there she watched the doors and listened carefully to the hall. The apartment, the office, and the car all had moments that felt tolerable, yet she spoke of no longer having a broad sense of ease anywhere in the world.

At night, Layla often woke abruptly and immediately checked whether she was safe. She would sit up, listen, and sometimes go from room to room before settling again, trying to reassure herself that the door was locked and the apartment quiet. Her husband noticed that she was sleeping in shorter stretches, and that she became alert at sounds that would previously have gone unnoticed. Unexpected noises-a sudden bang in the street, a dropped pan, a shout from outside-made her whole body tense. She described being on high alert whenever she heard loud or unanticipated sounds, as if her mind had already moved several steps ahead and was preparing for the next danger before her surroundings had even changed. In those moments, she was not thinking abstractly about the past; she was simply bracing herself, listening, and trying to determine whether the sound meant someone was coming or whether she needed to move.

Over time, these experiences altered the shape of her daily life in quiet but consequential ways. She began choosing routes and timings that reduced the chances of being alone, avoided lingering near doors and windows, and limited the places she would agree to stay after dark. At work, she remained competent, but colleagues noticed that she preferred controlled environments and that she became visibly unsettled by sudden interruptions. The emotional tone of her life also shifted. Layla said, with visible bitterness, that she used to be a happy person but now felt always miserable. She could remember enjoying ordinary things before the violence, but now that memory felt remote and almost embarrassing, as if it belonged to someone else. She also judged herself harshly for how little she seemed able to manage. Small disruptions-a delayed call, a change in plan, a loud noise, a stranger standing too close-felt overwhelming to her, and she said she could not deal with even the slightest upset. That sense of diminished capacity sat alongside a broader conviction that the world is a dangerous place, a conviction reinforced each time she found herself checking over her shoulder or waking in the night to see whether the apartment was still secure.

By the time she sought help, Layla was still functioning in many respects, but she was tired of living as though danger might be waiting just outside every door. She came to treatment because her vigilance had become exhausting, her sleep remained broken, and she no longer wanted her marriage and work to be organized around constant alertness. What frightened her most was the possibility that this way of living had become permanent, that she might never again feel like the person she used to be. More than anything, she hoped to recover some ordinary sense of safety in the places where she lived and worked, and to stop feeling as though every unexpected sound or passing voice could mean that she was once again being watched.
